||Combining agriculture and photovoltaics on the same land area gains in attention and political support in agrowing number of countries accompanied by notable research activities in France, USA and Korea, amongstothers. This study assesses the technical feasibility of agrivoltaic (APV), while it gives insights on how to designan APV system. Furthermore, it analyses the electrical yield and the behavior and productivity of four cropsgrown in Germany’s largest agrivoltaic research facility installed in 2016 near Lake Constance within theresearch project APV-RESOLA by Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE. The German design differsfrom most other agrivoltaic approaches by allowing for a wide range of machine employment, facilitated by avertical clearance of 5 m and a width clearance of up to 19 m. Crops cultivated under the APV system and on thereference feld under a crop rotation scheme include potato, celeriac, clover grass and winter wheat.The land use effciency measured by the Land Equivalent Ratio (LER) indicated a rise between 56% and 70% in2017 while the dry and hot summer in 2018 demonstrated that the agrivoltaic system could increase landproductivity by nearly 90%. Radiation simulations showed that deviating from full south by around 30◦resultedin equal distribution of radiation on ground level, representing the basis for the agrivoltaic design. Consideringclimate change and increasing land scarcity, our overall results suggest a high potential of agrivoltaics as a viableand effcient technology to address major challenges of the 21rst century.|

## **1. Introduction**

In light of climate change and rising world population, land scarcity will increase due to factors such as land-use change for agricultural land [1], energy demand [2] or other human needs [3] as well as additional factors which reinforce this development, like soil degradation [4]. These developments are leading to conflicts between land-use purposes [3], for instance between the agricultural and energy sector [5,6] Furthermore, recent progress in photovoltaic (PV) technologies and its vast potential for future energy generation [7–9] put increasing attention on the land-use footprint of large scale ground-mounted PV (GM-PV) [10,11].

One approach of minimizing the land-use footprint of GM-PV is agrivoltaics (or agrophotovoltaics, APV), a dual use of cropland for food production and PV power generation [12,13]. APV has the potential to increase the resilience of crops growing beneath the system. It can function as a protection system for plants against unfavorable weather conditions such as excessive sunlight or hail [14,15] and improve the water availability and water use efficiency respectively [16]. An advantageous implementation is assumed to be especially promising in countries with high land scarcity [13] or in arid climatic regions [17]. Firstly, the land can be used simultaneously by two sectors which eases the stress on scarce land. In this way APV is finding land for the energy transition of countries towards renewable energies [18] without reinforcing land use conflicts. Secondly, areas, which are inhospitable for

However, the benefits of APV are highly dependent on the area of implementation and the agricultural use beneath the system. More research is needed in this field as only little is known about how plants react to the changed climatic conditions which the APV system brings along. In the existing frameworks, the realization of APV is challenging in many countries as standards and policy schemes are missing [14]. However, some countries have already established certain support schemes. Governments in Japan, China, France, Massachusetts (USA), and Korea [14,19–22] have introduced policies promoting APV, leading to more than 2200 APV systems with an estimated capacity of at least 2.8 GW globally [14,23,24].

While Goetzberger and Zastrow developed the concept in 1981 [25], in Germany, one of the first practical APV applications can be found in Bavaria-, where the electrical engineering company, Guggenmos, has been cultivating different crops since 2008, under a PV system installed at a height of 1.5 m [26]. In 2013, the Weihenstephan-Triesdorf University of Applied Sciences installed the first APV research facility with a capacity of 28 kW in Bavaria, analyzing crop performance of Chinese cabbage and pointed cabbage [27]. So far, Fraunhofer ISE installed Germany’s largest APV research facility in Heggelbach, Southern Germany near Lake Constance with a capacity of 194,4 kW [28]. Today, the total installed APV capacity in Germany amounts for at least 10.6 MW with the largest share (10 MW) dedicated to ginseng production in Hesse [29].

While various recent paper analyzed the light distribution underneath solar panels with regard to module types, tilt angles and orientation of the system [24,30–33], there is a lack in the literature regarding the feasibility of agrivoltaic system with fixed tilted bifacial panels as well as the effect of different orientations apart from direct North-South or East-West orientation. This study aims to close this gap by assessing the technical feasibility of APV and providing insights on how to design an APV system based on light simulation with Radiance. Furthermore, it analyses the productivity of potato, celeriac, clover grass and winter wheat grown in an APV system and the electrical yield of the system. Accordingly, the LER values were computed based on the experimental results of the years 2017 and 2018. The system was installed within the project APV-RESOLA (Agrophotovoltaics – A Contribution to Resou rce-Efficient Land Use) in September 2016 on farmland of the Demeter farming community Heggelbach (south-east of Baden-Württemberg; 47[◦] 51[′] 14[′′] N, 9[◦] 8[′] 11[′′] E) [34]. The APV system design aims to achieve the best overall system output regarding practicability for farmers, social acceptance, as well as agricultural and electrical yields. With a vertical clearance of 5 m and a width clearance of up

to 19 m, the Heggelbach APV design allows for a much wider range of machine employment compared to most other APV approaches. The findings can be used as a manual for designing further APV systems.

Section 2 gives an overview of the theoretic background of designing an APV system. Therefore, it provides information about crop classification for APV, simulation for light distribution and row distance as well as introduces the concept of LER. Sections 3 presents preliminary simulation results and some electrical yield prediction. In Section 4 the final APV design and the main empirical findings during the first two years of operation with a focus on PV performance and land use efficiency are presented.

## **2. Theoretic background and simulations for designing an APV system**

## _2.1. Crop classification_

Generally, plants are capable of handling changing environmental conditions, at least to some extent [35]. Factors characterizing environmental conditions are light availability, temperature, water availability and wind, amongst others. Growth rates and yield for specific plants is determined by how much these factors deviate from the optimum conditions [35]. Agricultural crops, however, tend to tolerate smaller variations in environmental conditions compared to weeds, since they are bred to perform best under specific local conditions [36]. For simplification, in the remainder we only focus on light availability as the presuming most relevant factor for APV systems.

Impacts of the APV system on crop yields is one of the key issues associated with APV and an important concern of farmers [24]. However, there is still little information available about crops’ ability to tolerate and compensate low light levels in temperate latitudes [13]. In order to preselect promising species for APV cultivation, we divided Germany’s most important crops into three categories regarding their harvestable yield under moderate shading conditions (up to 40% light reduction). For more details on our categorization of Germany’s crops and crop growth models see Refs. [30,37,38]:

## _2.2. Simulations as a basis for the design of the APV plant_

All light simulations were carried out with Radiance [39], a backward ray-tracer for optical calculations in virtual environments developed by the University of California (Berkeley, CA). Taking both direct and diffuse fractions of irradiation into account, Radiance allowed simulating reflections from the ground in order to analyze electrical gains on the rear side of PV panels. To predict the overall electrical yield ZENIT, a software tool developed by Fraunhofer ISE [40] was used. It is based on the APV’ s specific configuration settings and the local irradiation conditions in Herdwangen-Schoenach, southern Germany (47[◦] 85[′] N, 9[◦] 13[′] E). Irradiation and meteorological data for the site was acquired from SolarGIS. The full year 2009 was used for the simulation since annual sums of global horizontal irradiance ( _Ghor_ ) and diffuse horizontal irradiance ( _Dhor_ ) are closest to the long-term average for the time period 2006–2015.[1 ] As a result, local irradiation conditions under the APV system represent the simulated amount of radiation reaching any point underneath the APV arrays during one year in 15-min time intervals for all daylight hours. While considering soiling losses of 0.5% per annum, we do not include losses caused by snow covering. Furthermore, ZENIT takes temperature coefficients, specific efficiency curves, maximum power points, and power limitation by the inverter into account, amongst others. By default, we assumed mismatching losses of 0.8%. Cable lengths and cross-sections resulted in additional resistive losses. As the prototype directly feds into the low-voltage grid, no transformer losses were considered.

## _2.5. Measuring the benefits of APV: Land Equivalent Ratio_

To quantify land use efficiency of intercropping systems, Mead and Willey [42] introduced the concept of the LER, which is frequently applied in agroforestry, aquaponics and recently also APV [13].

The LER can be defined as the relative land area that is required for mono-production in order to achieve the yield of dual land use. Following Willey [43], the LER is specified as the sum of the respective yield ratios of dual land use to mono land use: _Yielda_ ( _dual_ ) _Yieldb_ ( _dual_ ) _LER_ = _Yielda_ ( _mono_ )[+] _Yieldb_ ( _mono_ )

In what follows, _a_ and _b_ represent the cultivated crop and electricity, respectively. The concept of LER has been applied in order to compare the productivity of the Heggelbach APV system to standard mono cropping or GM-PV systems as well as to other APV systems.

Another important factor to be considered is the area losses that occur if some land cannot be cultivated due to the mounting structure of the APV system. This is particularly the case if the machinery used leaves uncultivated strips of land between the pillars. In fact, these area losses are much larger than the built-up area itself. In Heggelbach, only 0.23% of the total area was covered by mounting structure elements, whereas, during the first year, real losses amounted to 8.3% of the total area. Accordingly, we calculated the LER as follows: _Yielda_ ( _dual_ ) _Yieldb_ ( _dual_ ) _LER_ = _Yielda_ ( _mono_ )[+] _Yieldb_ ( _mono_ )[−][8] _[.]_[3% ]

LER _<_ 1 indicates that combined crop and energy production is less productive than separate production. In contrast, LER _>_ 1 indicates increased productivity in the APV system as compared to mono production.

## **3. Simulation results**

## _3.1. Orientation_

Conventionally oriented PV systems, towards 0[◦] S in the northern hemisphere, usually result in high heterogeneity of radiation at ground level leading to local differences in microclimate (e.g., humidity, temperature etc.) (see Fig. 2 first row at 0[◦] orientation). Hence, no adaption of the APV systems is likely to cause adverse effects of heterogeneous growth and ripening for most farming systems. In contrast, turning the system towards SW or SE (compare rows three and four with 30[◦] and 45[◦] ) reduces heterogeneity. Light on ground level between two PV panel rows is distributed more equal when increasing the deviation of the PV orientation from pure S particularly in months with high sun elevations in late spring/early summer. Fig. 2 depicts results for lower and higher row distances with a normalized row distance _d_ over module row width _w_ of 2.5 (left column) vs. 4.5 (right column). It shows the monthly sums of Ghor for March (03) to October (10), and yearly averages. Small squares (left side) indicate respective unshaded irradiation values. In the = first column orientation of the APV field is indicated (from azimuth 0[◦] facing South to azimuth = 45[◦] facing South-West). Ghor was calculated by Radiance.

Simulation results show that even deviations of 30[◦] result in quite homogeneous radiation distribution. It can be also seen that the trend of the homogeneity improves when the orientation of the panels diverges from 0[◦] S to 45[◦] SW or SE directions. However, there is hardly any additional difference between the last two alignments (30[◦] and 45[◦] ), which is why it can be assumed that even at 52[◦] there is not much difference to the radiation pattern shown. However, it would cause more losses in terms of energy generation. Moreover, another determinant factor is local conditions (e.g., orientation of field borders, direction of

travel of machinery, irrigation structures etc.) when the orientation is considered and they might require greater or less deviations. Maximum homogeneity of radiation at ground level could be achieved by single axis-tracked PV rows oriented N–S. Though, as in 2016 trackers were hardly economically viable in Germany, we did not consider them in the project.

## _3.2. Row distance_

As row distance increases, available radiation at ground level increases with higher irradiation during the summer months compared to winter months. Even at the smallest row distance, from May to July nearly 50% reaches the ground, whereas between November and January only 31% PAR and 38% PAR (S and SW orientation, respectively) reaches the ground. In addition, the extent of variation between the lower and upper margin of PAR at ground level decreases with increasing row distance. Looking at the S-facing system, the difference amounts to 18% at the smallest row distance compared to 6% at the largest row distance. SW orientation reduced the extent of variation to just 10% and 4%, respectively. During summer and on average over the year, orientation did not significantly affect the available radiation for crops. In Fig. 3 the PAR at ground level for S and SW relative to the row distance is presented (see equation (1)). The graph depicts means of months with highest (May to July) and least (November to January) radiation, respectively. Between calculated points, the function was interpolated.

For low row distances, biomass yields of the three categories tend to rise with increasing row distances (Fig. 4). Only category “PLUS” shows a slight optimum for summer-grown crops of around d = 4. Crop yields of winter cultivars decreased much more at higher module densities as compared to summer periods due to the lower relative PAR during winter.

With respect to summer months, expected yields of category “PLUS” were above 100% even at lowest row distance (Fig. 4). The PLUS category also achieved yields in summer months equal to unshaded conditions at row distances of 2.8 or 3.0 (for S- and SW-oriented systems), respectively, with higher yields at larger row distances. Crop yields in summer months from category “ZERO” were above 95% at d′ _>_ 3 _,_ whereas in winter months crops of this category achieved this yield level ′ ′ for d _>_ 4 _._ 7 and d _>_ 5 _._ 5 (S and SW), respectively. For MINUS crops, shading resulted in clear reductions of the harvestable yield at maturity. ′ In contrast, species achieved only 90% at d = 4 during summer months. To achieve 90% of the crop yield of an unshaded area, in winter months crops need row distances of at least 5.5 and 5 (S and SW), respectively, which is nearly three times the distance of a conventional system.

Fig. 5 presents the electrical yield of the two APV system orientations relative to the maximum yield achievable through an optimal techno ′ economic designed APV system oriented towards S (α = 0[◦] ) at d = 2 _._ 2. The graph depict means of the three months with highest (May to June) and lowest radiation (December to February), respectively. In summer months, the impacts of the APV system’s orientation on electrical yield were negligible, whereas during winter the S-facing system achieved a slightly higher electrical yield by about 5%.

To harness these results for defining the row distance of the Heggelbach APV design, we took into account at least three practical considerations. First and foremost, sustainable farming practices frequently rely on crop rotation [44], which is also the case for Heggelbach. Accordingly, we considered the needs and present farming methods of the Heggelbach community by agreeing on a crop rotation of potato, celeriac, clover grass, and winter wheat. The respective categories range from PLUS (potato), ZERO (celeriac, clover grass) to MINUS (winter wheat). Second, as this crop rotation does not encompass winter crops, we only considered summer periods. Third, crop yields of 80% in the APV system compared to unshaded conditions were targeted. This aim was based on discussions with farmers at Heggelbach and other

## **4. Practical implementation and results of the case study**

**Fig. 6.** Bird’s-eye view of APV testing and reference areas.

## _4.1. Engineering and installation of the APV system_

Based on the previously described theoretical foundations, the APV system technology was developed in cooperation with partners such as BayWa r. e. Solar Projects, Hilber GmbH, and the Demeter farming community Heggelbach. The research facility was installed in August and September 2016 on farmland in southern Germany. To ensure homogenous irradiation and due to the alignment of the field, the APV system is oriented towards SW with an azimuth of 52.5[◦] . The field encompasses two sections: the APV testing area and the unshaded reference area (Fig. 6).

For the foundation, a Spinnanker [46] system was implemented (Fig. 7). This foundation does not use concrete and follows the principle of tree roots. It consists of threaded steel rods with a diameter of 1 cm screwed into the circular ground plate. The bar length (2–8 m) and number of threaded rods (6 or 12) are variable, allowing flexible adaption to specific load and ground conditions. The exact rod lengths were determined by tests of pull-out resistance. These showed high levels of soil moisture, which required relatively long rods (4–8 m), and plates with 6 and 12 rods each were chosen because of difficult ground conditions.

The Spinnanker system offers advantages compared to the rope constructions or concrete foundations that are used in many other APV facilities in France and Japan. The anchoring rods can be quickly and easily installed with hand-held machines. Dismantling after the end of system operation is easy to perform without major adverse effects on the ground. Additionally, some parts of the system can potentially be reused afterwards. The dimensions of the mounting structure, i.e., clearance height and pillar distances, are determined by machine sizes. The largest harvesters need 5 m of clearance height, and sprayer booms are most typically 6 m wide. Accordingly, the distances between the pillars were chosen as a multiple of these measurements. In order to protect the

pillars from collisions with agricultural machines, ram protections have been installed. Ram protections are made of metal and are independently fixed to the ground in order to keep trailers, sprayer booms, etc. From getting caught on the pillar and damaging it.

For PV panels, we employed Sunmodule Bisun SW 270 duo bifacial modules (manufacturer: SolarWorld AG). These modules are covered by safety glass on both sides (Fig. 8). In Germany, legal requirements for PV applications in overhead areas only allow for conventional modules with a back foil in combination with additional safety precautions. Bifacial modules, however, are approved for overhead applications. Another advantage of bifacial modules is that more diffuse irradiation is available for the crops cultivated below them due to the small gaps between single solar cells within each module. Furthermore, electricity output is higher since the reflected radiation from the ground or crops can be used by the rear side of the PV module. On the other hand, these modules are still more expensive than conventional one-sided PV modules. Nevertheless, taking into account the higher power output and the associated electrical yield and the possible omission of safety precautions, the bifacial modules were the more profitable choice.

To protect the PV modules and the inverter against lightning which can be expected to strike the system about once every 30 years, several lightning protection rods with a length of 0.5 m were installed on the supporting structure. The length of the rods and the distance between them were calculated by using rolling spheres with a diameter of 90 m corresponding to lightning protection class III.

Non-representative preliminary studies showed that challenges might occur due to water dripping down from module edges: during fallow periods or periods with little vegetation, there might be a risk of soil erosion leading to the formation of gullies [47]. But to date, after three winters, no negative effects such as soil erosion have been detected so far. However, modifications to the construction can be implemented in the future whenever needed (e.g., rain gutters or distributors could be Table 2. installed). ## _4.2. Electrical yield during first year of operation and crop performance_

Over the first year, the measured solar irradiance amounted to 1217 kWh per m[2 ] which resulted in generation of 1265 kWh per installed kW peak. Hence, the total amount of electricity produced during the first year of operation was 246 MWh.

In comparison, a standard PV-GM plant in the same location would have generated approximately 295.4 MWh during the same period. Therefore, the electrical yield of the APV system was about 17% lower than the electrical yield in a reference scenario. ## _4.3. Results of land use efficiency_

Looking at the combined yields of electricity and harvestable products, LERs were found between 1.56 and 1.70 in 2017, and 1.67 and 1.87 in 2018 (Fig. 9). Compared to other mixed systems like in agroforestry, overall, these increases in productivity clearly represent an extraordinarily high level. In addition, the large differences between the two years indicated the extent to which agricultural yields depend on weather conditions with quite notable differences in temperature, precipitation and sunshine duration. In 2018, air temperature was significantly warmer with far less precipitation and much higher solar irradiation than the preceding year (Table 4). When precipitation is scarce, shading through APV can obviously become an advantage and may support higher crop yields. For three out of four species, winter wheat, potato and celeriac this resulted in higher crop yields of APV compared to the reference area. Only clover grass showed similar results for both years, which implies that APV does not give an advantage to clover grass even in drier years.

In the present study, the mean LERs of both years ranged from 1.71 (winter wheat) to 1.76 (both, celeriac and potato), which was clearly higher than results from [13]. They predicted, as conservative values, LERs between 1.19 and 1.43. Partially, though, the high LER of the Heggelbach system might result from bifacial modules and the higher vertical clearance compared to experiments of [13]. Both factors significantly affect the irradiation conditions of the APV system.

## **5. Discussion**

An optimized layout of an APV system has to meet several requirements. Within the APV-RESOLA project, we aimed at a holistic, interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary approach in order to develop a technological solution that can be considered as a meaningful compromise between all requirements at a specific location in southern Germany. Still, there remain open questions and uncertainties about the presented APV approach and the APV technology in general.

Row distance, as the main factor in the trade-off between electrical and agricultural yields, not only affects overall profitability, it also raises ethical questions such as how much yield losses society is willing to accept given the very productive soils available. While these aspects are mainly analyzed by the project partner - Institute for Technology Assessment and Systems Analysis [49], we accounted for this issue in technical terms by targeting at crop yields of at least 80% compared to unshaded crop yield. Taking area losses due to the mounting structure into account, this goal has only been reached for clover grass in 2017. In contrast, crop yield of celeriac, potato and winter wheat – at between 74.4% and 75% compared to the reference – was below this threshold. Disregarding these area losses, however, the results clearly indicate that crop yields could potentially reach between 82% and 94% if more efficient solutions for cultivation practices can be found. In 2018, however, harvestable yields of all four species exceeded the threshold considerably. These results validated our assumption, that APV is advantageous under dry and warm climatic conditions. In this context, the row distance implemented seems rather conservative.

In the light of climate change with its warmer and dryer weather conditions, and the high crop yields that are achieved in 2018 show that there might be a potential of reducing row distance in future applications.

Another critical aspect is crop choice. Typically, the optimal row distance for a specific location also depends on the cultivated crops. Moreover, large differences can be expected not only between different species, but also amongst varieties. The ongoing research project, however, is limited to four different crop species (potato, celeriac, clover grass, and winter wheat), thus many more crops and varieties should be analyzed in order to identify the impacts of APV. In addition, crop yields at different locations should be evaluated as the herein presented results are not necessarily transferable to other locations.

In this study, shading has been discussed as the only relevant parameter affecting crop performance of an APV system. However, crop productivity also depends on other factors such as air, soil, temperature, and precipitation [50,51]. Marrou et al. already observed these factors responding to APV [12]. In the Heggelbach project, all agricultural parameters were monitored by our partner, the University of Hohenheim, in order to understand and predict crop productivity under APV. For more detailed information see Ref. [24].

The proportion of electrical self-consumption is a crucial parameter representing a major impact on economic viability of an APV system, particularly for small systems. If electricity selling prices are lower than consumer prices, generally, a rising level of self-consumption increases viability. For further findings on economic viability of APV systems see Refs. [52,53].

Regarding the LER, land losses of the APV system are considerably smaller than estimated by, for example, Dupraz et al. [13], which was mainly driven by the large width clearance. We measured area losses (uncultivated area due to the mounting structure of the APV system) of about 8.3%, whereas Dupraz et al. [13] estimated 10%. However, 8.3% is still much more than just the built-up area of the APV system and is therefore a parameter that could be optimized. Obviously, from an economic point of view, this makes a strong case for manual or other cultivation practices that allow losses to be limited to the built-up area. Ecologically, though, these spared strips of land pave the way for increases in biodiversity as the natural vegetation remains rather unaffected within this area.

Overall, we obtained impressively high LERs. One reason for the occurrence of LERs that are too high or too low is if light penetrates from the sides of the APV system leading to border effects in eastern, southern, and western zones of the system with a higher PAR as expected. This seems particularly true due to the relatively small width of system (25.3 m) compared to the high vertical clearance (5 m). An irradiation map in the Annex shows these border effects. Accordingly, in the year 2017, border effects might have caused a higher LER than in case of without border effects since shade had a negative impact on agricultural yields. However, as in 2018 where the effect of shade was clearly beneficial for three out of four crops, the LER would have been even higher without the border effect or for a bigger scale system where the border effects

would be less influential. Against this background, the LER seems to be less affected by border effects but rather by the dry and hot summer of 2018. Nevertheless, there is still a need to investigate more crop species and varieties over several years in order to understand the interactions between weather conditions and APV on crop yields.

Unlike ordinary GM-PV systems, the installation of an APV system strongly depends on weather conditions. The soil has to be relatively dry to protect it from compaction, because crops should be able to grow on the field again shortly after the installation process. Therefore, installation activities are limited to drier weather conditions during summer or early fall. For the same reason, we used mobile driveways during the construction activities in order to avoid soil compression. As a result, the time frame for the construction of an APV system is much less flexible than for GM-PV systems, which can be set up at any time of the year and almost independently from weather conditions.

Regarding the potential of APV to contribute to the energy transformation in Germany, a first assessment of the APV potential in Germany recently found a technically feasible capacity of approximately 1700 GW [54]. Usual energy scenarios for Germany predict a PV capacity between 200 GW and 500 GW until 2050 [55]. This indicates that, in technical terms, APV appears eligible to provide sufficient PV capacity for the energy transformation in Germany without sacrificing arable land. Further and with respect to the physical dimensions of the presented Heggelbach APV design, these figures also imply that there is little need for aiming at very high vertical clearances and large row distances. In contrast, the vast availability of agricultural areas suggests putting the focus of future APV projects on agricultural applications that do not rely on large land machines in order to reduce the cost on mounting structure and installation.

## **6. Conclusion and outlook**

In this study, the technical feasibility of APV system was assessed while providing the analysis of design parameters such as the row distance and orientation of the facility, and their effects on the sunlight availability under the system. In that context, the virtual simulations were made; accordingly, the APV facility was constructed. Thereafter, the results of the operated facility were presented and the LER values

were computed.

The rise of high land-use efficiency as well as the overall technical, economic and social research results of the APV-RESOLA project [14,49] indicates a high potential of APV to address major challenges of the 21rst century. Particularly, the results of the dry and hot summer in 2018 demonstrated that APV bears the chance to enhance the resilience of farming systems against future drought. Accordingly, the technical potential of APV seems highest in arid and semi-arid climatic regions of the world with limited water resources and high solar radiation. In these regions, APV might reduce evapotranspiration and, hence, decrease irrigation needs, drought stress, and soil degradation [56,57]. Combining APV systems with water pumping, water treatment and irrigation systems, APV might be an eligible technology to restore degraded land or to revegetate desert areas. Furthermore, altered microclimate conditions might allow for cultivation of other crop species increasing biodiversity and resilience of the agricultural sector against climate change.

For the German case, after demonstrating the technical feasibility of APV, a coherent next step could be a small series of APV systems to gain further insights in business models, social acceptance and different agricultural applications, amongst others. This might also include tracked APV systems, PV modules with higher light transparencies, integration of water managements systems (e.g. for irrigation or rainwater harvest), the electrification of agricultural machinery, APV for large scale Hydrogen generation, and applications on specialty crops like hops, grapes, berries or orchards. For a broader dissemination of the technology, though, a specific regulatory framework appears indispensable to ensure economic viability.
